gmContextBlob.openingNarration:
The ladder shaft groans as you climb down to mid-deck, a long metallic sigh that seems to come from somewhere deeper than the hull plating should allow. The emergency lights out here run amber instead of white — half the fixtures on this level went dark two nights ago and nobody's fixed them yet. Your breath fogs faintly; environmental's been struggling to keep pace with the cryo bay's draw.

Mara Odinsen is waiting at the bottom of the ladder, arms crossed, a data slate tucked under one elbow like she's been standing there a while. "You seeing this?" she says, not quite a greeting, and taps the bulkhead beside her. A hairline crack runs along the seam, dusted with a faint rime of frost that shouldn't be there — condensation freezing in a gap that shouldn't exist on a ship this age, this maintained. Except it isn't maintained, not really, and you both know the captain's logs say otherwise.

Somewhere above you, the ship groans again, and four hundred and twelve people sleep on, unaware that the sound might be the last warning anyone gets.

messages.content: OOC: What do I know about this ship? About Mara?
OOC: What do I know about this ship? About Mara?

[OOC: Here's what Danny would actually know at this point, no rolls needed — this is just recap/orientation.]

**The ship — ESV Halbrecht:**
You've been aboard three weeks now, hauling freight and doing the unglamorous work of keeping four hundred and twelve colonists asleep while the ship gets them there. She's an old bird. The maintenance logs say she had a full refit before this run, but you've seen the actual state of the conduits in the lower deck, and "full refit" is not the phrase that comes to mind. Emergency lighting's been up on half the mid-deck since day four because the main grid keeps browning out, and nobody's given you a straight answer why. Long-range comms are down too — the captain says it's "scheduled maintenance," which is the kind of thing captains say when they don't want a follow-up question.

Layout-wise: three decks, one central ladder shaft connecting them, narrow and badly lit. Upper deck has the bridge, comms, the captain's quarters, and the engineering records terminal tucked aft of the bridge. Mid-deck is crew berths, the mess, medbay, and the cryo bay — a big cold chamber, blast-door sealed, holding all four hundred-plus colonists. Lower deck is cargo, the engine room, life support, and the aft airlock. You've noticed — because you've had to work near it — that there are stress fractures already visible in the hull plating around the engine room and life support. Nobody's flagged it officially. You have.

Six live crew total, including you and Mara. It's a skeleton run for a ship this size.

**Mara Odinsen:**
You've shipped with her before — she's solid, competent, not someone who spooks easy. She's aboard under a cargo-handler contract, and she's good at the job: trained hands with Zero-G work and general ship's athletics. But since before you even broke orbit, she's had a bad feeling about this run specifically. She doesn't trust the officers — any of them — and she's been quietly building something. You've caught her cross-referencing hazard-pay clauses against the manifest, asking pointed questions about evacuation protocol nobody asked her to ask. She hasn't said outright what she thinks is going on, but you know Mara well enough to know she doesn't do paranoia for sport. If she's circling something, there's usually a reason.

You don't have a stake in whatever she's chasing. Not yet.]
"Yeah, I see it," I say to Mara. "'Full refit,' my ass."

Mara doesn't look at you when she answers — she's got a panel cover off near the ladder shaft junction, running a thumb along a weld seam that's gone the wrong color.

"Full refit," she repeats, flat. "I pulled the work order myself before we broke orbit. Signed off by a yard supervisor whose license lapsed eight months prior. You want to know how I know that? Because I checked. Nobody checks. That's the whole trick." She lets the panel cover hang on its hinge and finally turns to you. "This ship shouldn't have cleared inspection. It cleared inspection. Someone wanted it to."

She jerks her chin toward the ladder shaft, down toward the lower deck. "There's a terminal upstairs, aft of the bridge. Engineering records. If the falsification goes deeper than one lazy signature, it's in there. I've been trying to get five minutes alone with it since we left dock." Her jaw tightens. "Captain doesn't let cargo handlers wander the upper deck unescorted. Wonder why."

She's watching you now, gauging something. "You in, or is this still my problem?"
"I don't like it," I say without committing. "Do we have the equipment to fix this? Might be a higher priority than chasing down the records."

Mara's mouth twists — not quite a smile. "Fix it. Sure." She taps the discolored weld with one knuckle, and it gives off a sound that's wrong, a little too hollow. "We've got patch kits rated for micro-fractures. Sealant foam, some structural tape that's better than nothing. What we don't have is a yard, a drydock, or replacement plating for a hull section that's been flexing wrong for God knows how long. If this is what I think it is — stress fatigue working its way through the frame — we can slow it. We can't fix it. Not out here."

She straightens up, wipes her hand on her coveralls. "And that's the thing that keeps me up, Danny. A patch job buys time. The records terminal tells us whether we're patching a ship that was supposed to make it, or babysitting a hull they already wrote off." She holds your eyes. "Those are different jobs. I'd like to know which one I'm doing before it decides for me."

Down the corridor, the lights flicker once — a half-second brownout, the kind you've both stopped flinching at — and steady again. Neither of you comments on it.

"So," she says. "Patch kit's in the lower deck lockup, by engineering. Terminal's upstairs, past the bridge, and I need someone running interference or a better reason to be up there than 'felt like it.' Pick one. I can't do both alone."
"Sure, I don't mind distracting know-it-all captains," I say with a grin. "Maybe he caught the latest Premier League scores on Risus 7 before we broke orbit."

That gets an actual laugh out of her — short, surprised, like it's been a while since anyone made her do that. "Risus 7. Right. I'm sure the captain's a football man." She's already moving, checking the corridor both ways out of old habit. "Give me ten minutes after you've got him talking. If he's the type to enjoy an audience, that buys me more — don't let him wrap it up early."

She heads for the ladder shaft, then pauses with one boot on the first rung. "And Danny — if the terminal's locked behind something more than a door, I'll signal. Don't come running if it goes loud. Just... know it went loud."

She climbs. You give her the ten minutes, then head for the bridge, working out in your head what a deckhand who's never cared about ship's business before is suddenly curious enough to ask about. The captain's a man who likes being asked things. That much you can use.

The bridge hatch is standing open when you get there — Captain Voss is alone at the nav station, half-lit by the glow of a course-plot he's been staring at longer than a routine check should take. He looks up when your shadow crosses the threshold, and for just a second, before his face resets into something professional, you catch what might be tiredness. Or might be something closer to guilt.

"Hauling something, or did you get lost?" he says.
I want to make small talk with the captain, ask him about football, ask him if he's flown a lot of colony gigs like this, anything to keep him occupied. Is there a roll for that?

No roll needed — this is just conversation, and the price of failure here isn't high, it's just how long you can hold his attention.

You lean against the hatch frame like you've got nowhere else to be. "Lost implies I had somewhere to be in the first place. Nah, just restless. Cryo shift's boring as hell when you're not the one sleeping through it." You nod at the plot on his console without really looking at it. "Hey, you catch anything before we broke orbit? Risus 7 was supposed to have a match going, some derby thing. Half the crew was arguing about it in the mess before launch."

Voss's shoulders come down half an inch — this is easier ground than whatever he was staring at. "Missed it. We shipped out two days early." He says it like it still needles him. "Company moved the window up. Didn't get a reason, just got a new departure time."

"Two days early," you say, keeping it light, just a deckhand making noise. "Must've been a hell of a scramble getting cargo loaded."

"You have no idea." He almost smiles, rubs at his eyes. "You do a lot of these long hauls?"

"First colony run. You?"

"Eleven years," he says, and there's something in how fast that number comes out — not proud, just tired, like he's said it to justify himself before. "This is the biggest ship I've had. Also the oldest." He catches himself, glances back at the plot, and the ease drains out of his face a little. "Anyway. Don't you have a shift?"

He's still talking, but you can feel him starting to want the conversation to end. If you want more time out of him, you'll need to either ask something that hooks his attention again or accept you're on borrowed minutes now.
"11 years is a long time. You ever have the company bump the schedule up on you like that before?"

The question lands somewhere it wasn't supposed to. Voss goes still for just a fraction of a second — not long, but you clock it, the way his hand stops moving on the console.

"Bumped up? Sure. Company does what the company does." He says it too fast, and then seems to hear himself say it too fast, because he adds, "Cargo manifests shift, insurance windows shift, whatever. Eleven years, you stop asking why." He turns back to the plot, and this time it's not idle — he's making a show of being busy. "This one's just... a bigger contract than usual. More eyes on it upstairs."

"Insurance windows," you repeat, like it's a throwaway. "That a thing that moves departure dates?"

He doesn't answer that one. Instead: "You said you had a shift." Not a question this time.

Whatever door was cracked open a second ago, he's closing it. He's not hostile — not yet — but the easy tiredness from a minute ago has hardened into something more careful, more aware of you as a person asking questions rather than a bored deckhand killing time. If Mara needed more minutes, you've bought a few, but you've also put yourself on his radar in a way you weren't before.
I shift my weight to the other foot, "Hey, you got a favorite team back on Risus?"

You let the insurance thread drop like it never mattered, easy as anything, and shift your weight to the other foot. "Hey, you got a favorite team back on Risus?"

It's clumsy — a little too obvious a pivot after where the conversation just was — and Voss's eyes flick to you for a second with something that isn't quite suspicion yet, more like recalibration. Like he's re-filing you from *bored deckhand* to *bored deckhand asking oddly specific questions right before asking about football.*

But he answers. "Kestrel Reach," he says, distracted, already turning half back to his console. "Wife dragged me to a match once, years back. Been stuck with them since." He taps something on the plot, closes a window that was open, and when he looks back at you his face has gone back to professional. Neutral. Done. "Look — I appreciate the company, but I've got a burn correction to finish before end of shift. You should get back to your post."

It's not unfriendly, but it's final. The window's closed. Whatever ease you had going with him a minute ago, it cooled the second insurance windows came out of your mouth, and no amount of small talk is opening it back up today. He watches you a beat longer than a captain dismissing a deckhand normally would — filing your face away for later, maybe — before turning fully back to his station.

You've been up here a while now. Long enough, hopefully, for Mara to have done whatever she needed to do.
"Sure thing, cap," I say with a nod and head back.

"Sure thing, cap," you say with a nod, and let yourself out of the bridge without hurrying — hurrying is the kind of thing a man like Voss notices twice.

The ladder shaft is dim as always, the emergency lighting throwing long amber stripes across the rungs. You climb down toward the deck below, half-expecting to find Mara waiting, and instead find the corridor near the engineering records terminal empty. No Mara. No signal.

Then you hear it — soft, from just past the bend, the particular quiet of someone trying not to make noise. You round the corner and find her crouched at the terminal alcove, a data slate in one hand, the terminal's access panel still lit and humming behind her. She doesn't look up right away. When she does, her face has the look of someone who found exactly what they were afraid they'd find.

"Two days," she says, low. "Voss said the launch got moved up two days, right? Well. The maintenance sign-off on the hull frame — the one that's supposed to certify structural integrity for a haul this size — it's dated *after* we broke orbit." She turns the slate toward you. Rows of timestamps, a signature block, a yard supervisor's ID that means nothing to you but clearly means something to her. "Somebody backdated an inspection that never happened, Danny. And there's a second file in here I haven't even opened yet — insurance schedule, keyed to hazard multipliers. I don't like what a hazard multiplier is doing on a hull certification terminal."

She's still crouched, still reading, and there's a stillness to her that's worse than her usual anger — like she already knows where this goes and is bracing for it anyway.

"You buy me a few more minutes, or do we need to be somewhere else right now?"
Wait, did I climb down to the mid-deck or are we still on the top deck?

You're still on the upper deck. The bridge and the engineering records terminal are both up here — the terminal sits aft of the bridge, same level, just around the corridor bend. You never had to take the ladder shaft down at all; it's a short walk from one to the other. Mara came up here the same way, climbing from mid-deck where you two started, and she's been working the terminal on this same deck the whole time you were talking to Voss.

So: you're both still topside, a stone's throw from the bridge hatch you just walked out of, which is exactly why she's asking if you can buy more time rather than relocate.
"Uh, I think we should go," I say and scratch the back of my head. "Small talk is not my strong suit. Sorry."

"Uh, I think we should go," you say, scratching the back of your head. "Small talk is not my strong suit. Sorry."

Mara doesn't argue. She's already thumbing the slate dark and pocketing it, moving with the quick economy of someone who's done this before — copy first, panic never. "Don't apologize, you got me the time I needed." She taps the terminal's access panel closed, wipes the log with a practiced swipe that makes the access history blink and reset to idle. "That's the best I can do to cover it. If he checks who logged in, he'll see a timestamp and no name attached. Won't hold up to real scrutiny, but it'll hold up to a captain who isn't looking hard yet."

She's on her feet, slate tucked inside her jacket, already moving for the ladder shaft. "We talk properly once we're somewhere he isn't. Move."

You fall in behind her. The corridor back to the ladder shaft is quiet — too quiet, the way it always is up here — and neither of you says anything else until you're both climbing down toward mid-deck, the bridge and whatever Voss is doing up there now well behind you.
"What did you find?" I ask her once we're back near the cryo bay.

The climb down puts you back in familiar territory — the mid-deck corridor outside the cryo bay's blast door, cold bleeding through the bulkhead even from here. Mara stops, glances back the way you came to make sure the shaft is clear above, then pulls the data slate back out.

"Okay." She keeps her voice low even though there's no one around. "The hull certification — the one that's supposed to say this ship is fit for a haul this size, four hundred plus souls in cryo — is backdated. Signed off *after* we'd already broken orbit, by a yard supervisor whose license lapsed eight months before that. That's not a clerical error, Danny. That's someone building a paper trail after the fact because the real inspection either didn't happen or it happened and failed."

She scrolls the slate, and her jaw sets tighter. "And there's a second file. Insurance schedule, keyed to hazard multipliers — I saw it, I didn't get time to open it before you knocked on the door for me. I don't like what a hazard multiplier's doing anywhere near a hull cert. Multipliers like that usually mean somebody's done math on how much a *loss* is worth. Cargo. Crew." She looks at you, and there's something under the anger now — something closer to dread. "Colonists."

She pockets the slate again, but her hand lingers on it like she doesn't quite trust it out of reach. "I need to actually open that insurance file. Somewhere safe, not standing in a corridor. But Danny — if I'm reading the shape of this right, this ship isn't just old and neglected. Somebody *decided* it was disposable. And they put four hundred and twelve people to sleep on it anyway."

Behind the blast door, faint and mechanical, the cryo bay's systems hum on, indifferent — pumps and chillers keeping four hundred and twelve people unconscious for a trip somebody may have already written off.
"Could we access those records from engineering?" I ask her.

Mara shakes her head. "Engineering's got a terminal, sure, but it's not networked to the bridge records the same way — different access tier. What I pulled came off the *engineering records* terminal specifically, aft of the bridge. That's the only place that file lives, as far as I've seen. Engineering proper would have maintenance logs, sure, repair schedules, parts requisitions — useful, but it's not going to have the hull cert or the insurance schedule. Those are bridge-adjacent. Company paperwork, not ship's engineering."

She thinks about it another second, turning the slate over in her hand. "Unless... whoever backdated that cert did it *from* engineering, remote terminal access. That's possible. I don't know their setup well enough to say for sure." She looks at you. "Why? You thinking there's a copy down there, or you thinking we need a second way in that isn't walking past Voss's door again?"

The cryo bay hums on behind the blast door, indifferent to all of it.

"Just trying to find another way in." I shrug. "But if that terminal on the upper deck is the only way, I don't mind punching Voss's lights out to get you access. Fella knows there's something fishy going on around here."

That gets a short, humorless laugh out of Mara — not because it's funny, but because for a second you sounded like you meant it.

"Don't tempt me." She rubs at her eyes, and for the first time since this started, she looks tired instead of just angry. "But no — not yet. Decking the captain gets us exactly one thing: a mutiny charge and a locked brig, on a ship where he's the only one with codes to half the systems we might need later. If it comes to that, it comes to that. But I'd rather have the whole picture before I burn that bridge. Pun intended."

She glances back down the corridor, toward the ladder shaft, like she's making sure nothing followed you down. "Right now the insurance file's the priority. I need somewhere quiet to actually open it — my berth, maybe, or the cargo bay if it's empty. Once I know what it says, we'll know whether this is 'report it when we hit the relay beacon' or 'this needs to stop right now.'" She pauses. "Given what I've seen so far, I'm not betting on the first one."

She starts walking, slower now, toward the ladder shaft that leads down to the lower deck. "You in for round two, or you want to sit this one out and let me read it alone?"
"In for a penny, in for a pound," I say with another shrug.

"In for a penny, in for a pound," you say with another shrug.

That gets the ghost of a real smile out of her — small, but it reaches her eyes this time. "Good. Because I'd rather have someone at my back who already knows what I know than have to explain it twice." She leads the way to the ladder shaft, and you climb down together, past mid-deck and on toward the lower deck, the air growing warmer and closer to the engine hum the further down you go.

Her berth is a cramped closet of a room — a bunk, a locker, a fold-down desk barely wide enough for the slate. She dogs the door behind you both, which on a ship this old means wedging a boot heel of a bar into the frame latch rather than any real lock, and sits on the edge of the bunk with the slate balanced on her knee.

"Okay," she says, mostly to herself. "Let's see what we bought."

Her thumb hovers over the file. Insurance schedule, hazard multiplier, still locked behind a second layer of access encoding she didn't have time to crack topside.

"This one's going to take longer," she mutters, fingers already moving across the slate's input, working the encoding manually rather than through the terminal that's no longer in front of her. "Give me a few minutes. And Danny — if this says what I think it's going to say, we're going to need to talk about what we do next. Really talk. Not football."

The room is quiet except for the tick of her fingers on the slate and the distant thrum of the engines through the deck plating. Somewhere far below, or maybe just in your head, you think you hear the hull creak — long, low, and tired.
I wait patiently for Mara to do her work.

You lean against the wall by the door, arms crossed, and just let her work. The slate's screen throws pale light up across her face, her thumb tracing through screen after screen of nested menus, muttering things under her breath you can't quite follow — "no, that's not it, that's a routing key, not—"

Minutes stretch. The engine hum doesn't change. Somewhere below you, faint through the deck plating, something groans — metal settling, or metal complaining, you've stopped being able to tell the difference three weeks in.

Finally Mara sits back, and it's not the look of someone who cracked it clean. "Encoding's tougher than I figured — this isn't standard company boilerplate, somebody actually bothered securing this one properly, which tells you something on its own." She rubs at her temple. "I'm not locked out. But I'm going to be at this a while longer than I thought, and I don't want to rush it and trip something that locks the file for good."

She glances up at you. "You don't have to babysit me for this part. I'm not going anywhere — door's braced, and this could take another hour easy. You want to make yourself useful, go check on that patch kit situation you brought up earlier, or just get some air. I'll signal you the second I've got it open." She's already bent back over the slate, half her attention already gone from the room again.

The hum of the ship goes on around you both, patient and untrustworthy.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.

You leave Mara hunched over her slate and head down to the lower deck stores, where the patch kits live in a locker that hasn't seen a manifest audit in longer than it should have. Sealant foam canisters, rolls of structural tape rated for micro-fractures, a couple of hand-crank injectors for getting foam into places fingers can't reach. You take what you can carry.

The walk back up to mid-deck and around toward the cryo bay bulkhead takes a few minutes. Up close, the stress fractures are worse than they looked from a glance — hairline cracks spidering along a weld seam where the bulkhead meets the deck plating, the metal around them faintly discolored, like it's been flexing under a load it wasn't built for. When you press a hand flat against the plating, you can feel a vibration in it that shouldn't be there, a low shudder that doesn't quite sync with the engine hum.

You get to work. It's slow, unglamorous labor — scraping old sealant away, laying foam into the cracks, taping over the worst of it, working your way down the seam one meter at a time.
